chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ismail ibn Marrar and someone else, from Yunus, from some of his companions, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:

When a man hears the testimony but was not called as a witness upon it, then he is with the choice: if he desires he testifies, and if he desires he remains silent — except when he knows of an oppressor, then he testifies, and it is not permissible for him not to testify.

key_terms.الشَّهَادَة: testimony — the act of bearing witness, a legally significant act in Islamic law (fiqh) with strict conditions for validity
key_terms.الظَّالِم: the oppressor — one who commits injustice (zulm); knowledge of an oppressor's wrongdoing creates a positive duty to testify
key_terms.الْخِيَار: option/discretion — the legal right of choice; here meaning the person is not legally compelled

ai.seo_question: Is it obligatory to testify if you overheard testimony but weren't formally called as a witness in Islamic law?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (AS) establishes a key rule of voluntary testimony in Islamic jurisprudence: a person who happens to overhear a testimony without being formally summoned as a witness retains the discretion to testify or remain silent. However, this discretion is overridden when the person has knowledge of injustice perpetrated by an oppressor — in that case, testifying becomes a religious obligation and remaining silent is forbidden. This ruling was delivered to jurists in Kufa and Medina navigating the court systems of the Abbasid era, where the distinction between obligatory and permissible testimony had profound implications for social justice.
